CausalChain: NAFLD induces mitochondrial dysfunction -> Increased ROS production activates Nrf2 via Keap1 modification -> Impaired autophagy leads to p62 accumulation -> p62 displaces Keap1, sustaining Nrf2 activation -> Chronic Nrf2 signaling promotes metabolic reprogramming (anabolic shift and anti-apoptosis) -> Favorable environment for malignant transformation (HCC)
Hypothesis: In NAFLD, impaired autophagy leading to p62 accumulation sustains Nrf2 activation, which in turn reprograms hepatocyte metabolism toward a pro-tumorigenic state, thereby driving the progression from fatty liver disease to hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Recent observations indicate that while transient Nrf2 activation is protective against oxidative stress-induced liver injury, chronic activation due to impaired autophagy may drive metabolic reprogramming that predisposes hepatocytes to malignant transformation. Here, we propose that in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), mitochondrial dysfunction and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) induce Nrf2 activation via Keap1 modification. Concurrently, defective autophagy leads to the accumulation of the selective autophagy receptor p62, which competitively binds Keap1, further sustaining Nrf2 activation. Over time, this persistent Nrf2 signaling could shift hepatocyte metabolism toward anabolic processes and anti-apoptotic states, thereby facilitating the progression from benign steatosis to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). This integrative hypothesis highlights a potential link between autophagic regulation, redox homeostasis, and tumorigenesis in liver disease.
